questions.q: A field officer drafts a census form for a village. Which of her proposed questions is NOT one of the examples the chapter gives of information the Indian census collects from individuals?
questions.a: How many hours does the person sleep each day?
o: How many hours does the person sleep each day?
How many members are there in the person's family?
Which languages does the person speak at home?
What is the person's current employment status?

questions.q: Differentiate between the size of a population and its structure, using the margin note, and give one planning question that each could help to answer.
questions.a: Size is how many people live in a place; structure is how the population is made up by characteristics such as age, gender and education. Size helps answer how many people a service must reach in all; structure helps answer which kind of service, such as schools or healthcare, is needed.
s: Distinguishes size (how many) from structure (how made up by age, gender, education)
Gives one planning question for each

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
1. In India the census is generally conducted every five years to assess the total population and its characteristics.
2. The census collects from individuals details such as marital status, languages spoken and income levels.
3. Fig. 6.2 names size, pattern and trend, and structure and composition as the three components of demography.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A town had 50,000 people in 2005 and 50,000 in 2025 (illustrative figures). In 2005, 34 per cent were under 15, 61 per cent were aged 15 to 64 and 5 per cent were above 65. In 2025 the shares are 22, 62 and 16 per cent. Assume the town's schools had exactly enough seats for the children of 2005. The council can fund only one project this year: a new school building or more healthcare facilities.
(a) How many children and how many persons above 65 did the town have in each year?
(b) How many school seats are now unused?
(c) Predict which service the chapter's reasoning says is falling short.
(d) Decide which project to fund and give two reasons from your figures.
questions.a: (a) 2005: 17,000 children and 2,500 above 65. 2025: 11,000 children and 8,000 above 65. (b) 17,000 - 11,000 = 6,000 seats unused. (c) Healthcare facilities, because the proportion of the elderly is higher. (d) Healthcare facilities: the number above 65 has risen by 5,500, while 6,000 school seats already stand empty, so a new school would add nothing the town lacks.
s: Part (b): 6,000 unused seats
Part (c): healthcare facilities, from the higher elderly share
Part (d): healthcare, with the rise of 5,500 and the 6,000 empty seats as reasons

questions.q:
(a) State what the census is, in the chapter's definition.
(b) Using (a), explain why a careful survey of 200 households in one locality is not a census.
questions.a: (a) The census is the process of collecting, compiling, analysing and disseminating demographic, economic and social information of all persons in a country or a well-defined part of it at a specific time. (b) The survey covers only some households, not all persons, so it does not meet the 'all persons' part of the definition.
s: (a) Defines the census as covering all persons of a country or a well-defined part at a specific time
(b) Explains that 200 households leave out most persons, so it is not a census

questions.q: Write a situation, with your own illustrative figures, in which a district's demographic information would lead its planners to build a new hospital wing before a new school. Show the figures and the chapter's reasoning.
questions.a: Sample: In District D (illustrative), of 1,00,000 people only 9,000 are children under 15, while 22,000 are above 65. The chapter says that a higher proportion of the elderly means more facilities for healthcare are required, whereas many young children is what calls for more schools. Since the share of children is small and the share of the elderly is large, the hospital wing should come first.
s: Gives figures showing a small child share and a large elderly share
States the chapter's link: more elderly means more healthcare facilities
Explains why the school is less urgent

questions.q:
A student writes in her notebook: 'Knowing a country's population size and structure helps it to allocate and manage its resources.' Justify this sentence with examples.
(a) Give one example each for infrastructure, for a municipal service and for employment.
(b) Give one example of how a business uses the same kind of information.
(c) Say which of your examples would change first if the share of elderly people in the town doubled, and in which direction.
questions.a: (a) Infrastructure: many young children mean more schools are needed. Municipal service: the number of residents decides how much water, energy and waste management a town must provide. Employment: a higher proportion of young working-age people means a greater need for gainful employment generation. (b) A business assesses customers by age, gender and income to create products that match their needs. (c) The healthcare example: a higher proportion of the elderly means more facilities for healthcare are required, so the need rises, while the school example would weaken.
s: Gives a valid infrastructure example
Gives a valid municipal service example
Gives an employment example
Gives a business example using age, gender or income
Says healthcare need would rise with more elderly people

questions.q: The census collects many fields. Choose any three from the chapter's list and, for each, say one decision the answer could help a government or a business make.
questions.a: Sample: Age helps decide whether schools or healthcare facilities are needed. Occupation, or employment status, helps judge how much gainful employment must be generated. Income, together with age and gender, helps a business create products that match what people can buy.
s: Names three fields that are in the census list
Links each field to a distinct decision
Keeps the decisions to those the chapter describes

questions.q: Over twenty years the share of people aged 15 to 64 in a city has risen from 55 to 68 per cent, while the share above 65 has stayed small. By the chapter's reasoning, what should the city's planners expect to need most?
questions.a: Gainful employment for a larger working-age population
o: Gainful employment for a larger working-age population
More schools, since children must be a growing share
Facilities for healthcare, since elderly people are many
Fewer municipal services, since most residents are adults

questions.q:
(a) The margin note defines the working-age population by an age band. State the band.
(b) A town has 20,000 people, of whom 13,600 are in that band. Find the share, and say what the chapter says a high share of young working-age people implies.
questions.a: (a) 15 to 64 years. (b) 13,600 / 20,000 = 68 per cent. A higher proportion of young working-age people implies a greater need for gainful employment generation.
s: (a) States 15 to 64 years, and (b) computes 68 per cent
(b) States the implication: a greater need for gainful employment generation

questions.q: A ward's population rose by 800 in one year. Which of the following could NOT, taken alone, explain that rise according to the way the chapter says populations change?
questions.a: More deaths than births, with nobody moving in or out
o: More deaths than births, with nobody moving in or out
More births than deaths, with nobody moving in or out
More people moving in than moving out, with births equal to deaths
More people moving in, which outweighs deaths being higher than births

questions.q: One firm sells school uniforms and another sells reading glasses for elders. Which single characteristic of a district's people, among those the chapter names for businesses, separates the customers of the two firms best?
questions.a: Age
o: Age
Gender
Income
The family's religion

questions.q: True or False? 'Two towns with exactly the same population can need very different mixes of schools, healthcare facilities and jobs.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The needs depend on the structure and composition of the population (how many are children, working-age or elderly, and so on), not on the size alone, so equal totals can still need different services.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: needs follow structure and composition, not size alone

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A business can use information on the age, gender and income of its potential customers to decide what products to create.
Reason (R): Fig. 6.2 names size, pattern and trend, and structure and composition as the three components of demography.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: A new colony of 5,000 homes is approved at the edge of a town. Which set of services does the chapter list as municipal services that demographic information helps a government plan?
questions.a: Water, energy and waste management
o: Water, energy and waste management
Schools, hospitals and employment
Taxes, pensions and healthcare costs
Water, roads and maternity wards

questions.q:
(a) A town of 60,000 people is joined by 15,000 new residents. Which municipal services named in the chapter will feel the larger number first?
(b) For this planning of water, energy and waste management, is the total number of people enough, or must the planner also know their ages? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Water, energy and waste management, because more residents use more of each. (b) For these services the total number of residents is the main guide, since every person needs water and produces waste; the ages matter more when the choice is between schools, healthcare facilities and jobs.
s: (a) Names water, energy and waste management
(b) Says size is the main guide here and structure matters for choosing schools, healthcare or jobs

questions.q: Meena says: 'A town with many elderly people needs more healthcare facilities, and the same age figures tell the town nothing about employment.' Judge her statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is correct: a higher proportion of the elderly means more facilities for healthcare are required. The second half is wrong: the same age figures show the share of young working-age people, and the chapter says a higher proportion of them implies a greater need for gainful employment generation.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts that many elderly people mean more healthcare facilities
Rejects the second half: the age shares also show the need for employment generation

questions.q: Rohan says: 'Demography only counts how many people live in a place, so a school principal has no use for it.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. Demography is not only counting: it studies the composition of the population by age, sex, occupation and religion and how it changes over time. A principal can use the number of young children in her area to see whether more schools are needed, which is the chapter's own example.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Shows demography studies composition and change, not only numbers
Gives the principal's use: many young children means more schools are needed

questions.q:
In one year a town of 12,000 people (illustrative) recorded 180 births and 90 deaths; 400 people came to live in it and 150 left it.
(a) Find the town's population at the end of the year.
(b) Which caused more of the net change, births and deaths together or movement of people? Show the two figures.
(c) The town planner counted only births and deaths. Explain, using the chapter, why her estimate of next year's population would be too low.
questions.a: (a) 12,000 + 180 - 90 + 400 - 150 = 12,340. (b) Births minus deaths added 90, while movement added 400 - 150 = 250, so movement caused more of the change. (c) The chapter names three causes of change in a population: births, deaths and the movement of people. Ignoring movement leaves out the 250 net arrivals, so her estimate would be too low.
s: Computes 12,340
Shows 90 from births and deaths against 250 from movement and names movement
Explains that movement is the third cause the planner left out

questions.q:
Ward R (illustrative figures) has 30,000 people: 4,500 under 15, 19,500 aged 15 to 64 and 6,000 above 65. The census records that 4,680 of the 19,500 are not employed and are looking for work. Assume the ward's schools have seats for 6,000 children. The council can fund one project this year: a programme to create jobs or a new primary school.
(a) Name the census fields that give the number looking for work.
(b) What share of the 15 to 64 group is looking for work?
(c) How many school seats are unused?
(d) Decide which project to fund and say what the chapter says a large working-age population implies.
questions.a: (a) Employment status (together with age, which sets the group). (b) 4,680 / 19,500 = 24 per cent. (c) 6,000 - 4,500 = 1,500 seats are unused. (d) The job-creating programme: a quarter of the working-age group has no work and the schools already have spare seats, and the chapter says a higher proportion of young working-age population implies a greater need for gainful employment generation.
s: Part (a): employment status and age
Part (b): 24 per cent
Part (c): 1,500 seats
Part (d): jobs programme, citing the unemployed share, spare seats and the chapter's link to employment generation

questions.q: A town's planners find that the share of elderly people in its population is high. According to the chapter, which should the town plan to provide more of?
questions.a: Healthcare facilities
o: Healthcare facilities
Primary school places
Jobs for young working-age people
Crèches for infants

questions.q:
Fig. 6.6 gives the world's 8.2 billion people of 2025 by region, including Asia 4.8 billion, Africa 1.5 billion, Europe 744.3 million and Northern America 387.5 million. Fig. 6.5 gives India as 1460 million in 2025.
(a) Find Asia's share of the world, to one decimal place.
(b) Find the combined share of Asia and Africa.
(c) Find the combined share of Europe and Northern America.
(d) Find India's share of Asia's population.
(e) State what the four shares together tell you about where the world's people live.
questions.a: (a) 4.8 / 8.2 = 58.5 per cent. (b) 6.3 / 8.2 = 76.8 per cent. (c) 1.1318 / 8.2 = 13.8 per cent. (d) 1.46 / 4.8 = 30.4 per cent. (e) Over three-quarters of the world's people live in just two regions, Asia and Africa, and India alone has nearly a third of Asia's people, while Europe and Northern America together hold just under a seventh.
s: Asia 58.5 per cent
Asia and Africa 76.8 per cent
Europe and Northern America 13.8 per cent
India's share of Asia 30.4 per cent
Draws the conclusion about concentration of the world's people

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the term in Column B that fits it.
Column A: 1. A forecast of the 2050 world population made from present trends  2. India going ahead of China in 2023  3. Italy's population getting smaller  4. Nigeria's population still rising fast
Column B: a. a shrinking population  b. a projection  c. the world's most populous country  d. a continuing rapid rise
A student says: 'India was already the world's most populous country in 2022.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: No: the chapter says India passed China only in 2023
o: No: the chapter says India passed China only in 2023
Yes: India's population has always been larger than China's, so it led in every year before 2023 as well
Yes: the chapter says India went ahead of China in 2011, when its population reached 1210 million
No: the chapter says India passed China in 2025, once its population reached 1460 million

questions.q:
(a) Fig. 6.3 gives India as 144 crore in 2024, and Fig. 6.5 gives 1460 million in 2025. Express 144 crore in millions (1 crore = 10 million).
(b) What does the difference from 1460 million mean, and what must a reader keep in mind when comparing the two figures?
questions.a: (a) 144 crore = 1440 million. (b) The difference is 20 million. It comes from the two figures belonging to different years, 2024 and 2025, so the reader must compare figures of the same year, or say which year each belongs to.
s: (a) 1440 million
(b) 20 million difference explained by the different years

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
1. World population grew from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8.2 billion in 2025.
2. According to United Nations projections, world population will peak at 9.7 billion in 2050 and then decline.
3. In 2025 Asia, with 4.8 billion people, was the most populous region of the world.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A town's number of births has stayed the same for twenty years, yet its population keeps rising although nobody has moved in or out. Using the chapter, suggest one reason, and say what it shows about the causes of population growth.
questions.a: Improved healthcare lets people live longer, so fewer people die each year and the population grows even with unchanged births. This shows that growth can come from falling deaths and not only from rising births.
s: Gives improved healthcare enabling people to live longer
Concludes that growth can come from fewer deaths and not only more births

questions.q: A health worker's diary for a village in Assam notes four changes since 1950: (i) children are given vaccines at the health centre; (ii) most homes now get safe tap water and have toilets; (iii) packets of oral rehydration solution are kept in every anganwadi; (iv) fewer children die of malaria and diarrhoea. Link any three of her entries to the reasons the chapter gives for the rapid growth of world population, and say what the three have in common.
questions.a: (i) Vaccines are one of the medical advancements the chapter names. (ii) Better water and sanitation facilities reaching more people is another reason. (iii) Oral rehydration solution is another named medical advancement. (iv) Fewer child deaths from malaria and diarrhoea is the chapter's own fourth point. What they have in common is that each lowers deaths, so more people survive and the population grows.
s: Matches three entries correctly to the chapter's reasons
Names the reason each one illustrates
States the common effect: fewer deaths, so more survive

questions.q: The world's 8.2 billion people of 2025 were spread by region as Asia 4.8 billion, Africa 1.5 billion, Europe 744.3 million and Northern America 387.5 million. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Asia and Africa together hold more than three-quarters of the world's people
o: Asia and Africa together hold more than three-quarters of the world's people
Asia alone holds more than three-quarters of the world's people
Africa alone holds more than a third of the world's people
Europe and Northern America together hold more than a quarter of the world's people

questions.q: Kavya says: 'India went ahead of China in 2023, but in 2024 the two were still close: India's lead over China was only 4 crore, a small part of China's total.' Fig. 6.3 gives the 2024 populations as India 144 crore, China 140 crore and the United States 33 crore. Test her claim against these figures and give a verdict.
questions.a: Yes. Fig. 6.3 gives India 144 crore and China 140 crore in 2024, so the lead is 4 crore, which is under 3 per cent of China's 140 crore (4 / 140 = 2.9 per cent). Her claim is also consistent with the chapter saying India surpassed China in 2023.
s: Verdict: Yes, she is right
Computes the 4 crore lead from 144 and 140
Shows it is small against China's total, about 2.9 per cent

questions.q: A student writes: 'India added more people in 1951 to 1961 than in 2001 to 2011.' Fig. 6.5 gives India's population as 361 million in 1951, 439 million in 1961, 1020 million in 2001 and 1210 million in 2011. Show that the student's statement cannot be right.
questions.a: From Fig. 6.5, the addition from 1951 to 1961 is 439 - 361 = 78 million. The addition from 2001 to 2011 is 1210 - 1020 = 190 million. Since 78 million is less than 190 million, India added far fewer people in 1951 to 1961, so the statement is impossible.
s: Computes 78 million for 1951 to 1961
Computes 190 million for 2001 to 2011
Compares them and concludes the statement cannot hold

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter says growth in world population has slowed over time, which means the world's population is already falling.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Growth has slowed, but the population is still rising: it was 8.2 billion in 2025, is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, and is projected to peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s before it declines.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it is still rising and is projected to peak by the mid-2080s before a gradual decline

questions.q: A student says: 'World population grew rapidly after 1950 because many more babies were born every year.' Which assessment agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Not supported: the chapter ties the growth to medical advances, better water and sanitation and fewer child deaths, not to more births
o: Not supported: the chapter ties the growth to medical advances, better water and sanitation and fewer child deaths, not to more births
Supported: the chapter says the rapid growth came from a rise in the number of babies born each year
Supported: the chapter says the growth came only from economic prosperity reaching more people
Not supported: the chapter says the growth came from large numbers of people moving between countries

questions.q: A news report says: 'World population will be 9.7 billion in 2050.' Which rewording is most faithful to the chapter?
questions.a: World population is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, an estimate based on present trends
o: World population is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, an estimate based on present trends
World population has already reached 9.7 billion by 2050, as the census has counted every person in the world
World population will peak at 9.7 billion in 2050 and then fall steadily from that year onwards, as births drop
World population is certain to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, whatever happens to births and deaths in between

questions.q:
(a) Find the average yearly addition to world population from 1950 to 2025, using 2.5 billion and 8.2 billion, in millions.
(b) Find the same for 2025 to 2050 using 8.2 billion and 9.7 billion. What does the comparison show?
questions.a: (a) 5.7 billion over 75 years is 76 million a year. (b) 1.5 billion over 25 years is 60 million a year. The yearly addition is smaller in the later period, which agrees with the chapter's statement that growth has slowed.
s: (a) 76 million a year and (b) 60 million a year
Concludes the later addition is smaller, matching 'growth has slowed'

questions.q:
Use the India figures of Fig. 6.5 in millions: 1991 - 846, 2001 - 1020, 2011 - 1210.
(a) Find the additions in 1991 to 2001 and in 2001 to 2011.
(b) Express each addition as a percentage of the population at the start of that decade, to one decimal place.
(c) Which decade added more people, and which grew faster as a percentage?
(d) Explain why a larger addition can go with a slower percentage growth.
questions.a: (a) 1020 - 846 = 174 million; 1210 - 1020 = 190 million. (b) 174 / 846 = 20.6 per cent; 190 / 1020 = 18.6 per cent. (c) 2001 to 2011 added more people, but 1991 to 2001 grew faster as a percentage. (d) Each addition is measured against a bigger starting population, so a larger number of people can still be a smaller fraction of the base.
s: Additions 174 and 190 million
Percentages 20.6 and 18.6
Names the larger addition and the faster percentage correctly
Explains the effect of the larger base

questions.q:
China's population peaked at 1.43 billion in 2022 according to the chapter, and Fig. 6.3 gives China 140 crore in 2024; Fig. 6.3 gives India 144 crore in 2024. Fig. 6.5 gives India 1210 million in 2011 and 1460 million in 2025. The figures are rounded, so the yearly changes are only illustrative. A student forecasts: 'if China keeps falling by the same amount each year as between 2022 and 2024, and India keeps adding the same amount each year as between 2011 and 2025, then India's lead will keep growing steadily'.
(a) Find China's yearly fall in crore between 2022 and 2024.
(b) Find India's yearly addition between 2011 and 2025 in crore, to two decimal places.
(c) On the student's assumption, what would India's lead over China be, in crore, three years after 2024? Give one decimal place.
(d) Set China's side aside and consider only India. The chapter says growth in world population has slowed and that India's fertility rate is now below replacement level. Say whether this makes the student's forecast of (c) more likely to be too high or too low, and why.
questions.a: (a) 143 - 140 = 3 crore in two years, so 1.5 crore a year. (b) 250 million in 14 years is 17.86 million, that is 1.79 crore a year. (c) The lead in 2024 is 4 crore and grows by 1.5 + 1.79 = 3.29 crore a year, so after three years it is 4 + 9.86 = 13.9 crore. (d) Too high, or more exactly more likely to be too high. If India's yearly additions keep slowing as fertility stays below replacement level, India will add less than 1.79 crore a year, so the lead will grow more slowly than the student assumes.
s: Part (a): 1.5 crore a year
Part (b): 1.79 crore a year
Part (c): 13.9 crore
Part (d): too high, because India's yearly additions are likely to keep falling

questions.q:
(a) Name the three countries the chapter says are already seeing shrinking populations.
(b) The chapter says India's population 'is growing for now'. What does the phrase 'for now' warn the reader about?
questions.a: (a) China, Japan and Italy. (b) It warns that India's growth is not expected to last: the chapter says growth in the world has slowed, India's fertility rate is below replacement level, and a population can stop growing and then fall.
s: (a) Names China, Japan and Italy
(b) Explains that the present growth is not permanent, using slowing growth or below-replacement fertility

questions.q: China is second on the graph of the world's most populous countries for 2024, with 140 crore, yet the chapter says its population is already shrinking. Which explains how both can be true?
questions.a: The graph counts people in one year, while 'shrinking' describes how that number is changing over time
o: The graph counts people in one year, while 'shrinking' describes how that number is changing over time
The graph was drawn before the year in which China's population began to shrink, so it still shows China's earlier larger population
The graph counts only people of working age, so a fall in the total number of people cannot be shown on it
The graph and the chapter must disagree, since a country whose population is shrinking cannot still rank second in size

questions.q:
Two classmates made posters on world population.
Poster 1: 'World: 2.5 billion (1950); 8.2 billion (2025); 9.7 billion expected by 2050. UN projections: peak of 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s, then gradual decline.'
Poster 2: 'World: 2.5 billion (1950); 8.2 billion (2025); 9.7 billion is the peak, reached in 2050, after which growth has stopped and the population falls.'
(a) Which poster agrees with the chapter?
(b) State the two errors in the other poster.
(c) By what factor did world population multiply from 1950 to 2025, to one decimal place?
(d) Give two reasons from the chapter for the rapid growth that produced the factor in (c).
questions.a: (a) Poster 1. (b) Poster 2 calls 9.7 billion the peak, but 9.7 billion is only the expected figure for 2050 and the peak is 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s; and it says growth has stopped, but the chapter says growth has slowed, not stopped, and the population keeps rising until the peak. (c) 8.2 / 2.5 = 3.28, about 3.3 times. (d) Any two: antibiotics, vaccines or oral rehydration solution; better water and sanitation reaching more people; fewer child deaths from malaria and diarrhoea; the benefits of economic prosperity reaching more people.
s: Part (a): Poster 1
Part (b): both errors, 9.7 as the peak and growth having stopped
Part (c): 3.3 times
Part (d): two valid reasons from the chapter

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's population is growing for now, according to the chapter.
Reason (R): India's fertility rate is above the replacement level of 2.1.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Anil says: 'If a country's fertility rate is above 2.1 its population will definitely grow, and if it is below 2.1 it will definitely shrink.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The direction is right: above 2.1 the population is likely to grow and below 2.1 it might shrink over time. But the chapter says 'likely' and 'might', not 'definitely', and the change comes gradually over years, so he overstates it.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts the direction of the rule: above 2.1 growth, below 2.1 shrinking
Corrects 'definitely' to 'likely' and 'might', over time

questions.q: True or False? 'Birth rate and fertility rate are two names for the same measure.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 population in a year, while the fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime. They are closely linked, but they are different measures.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: births per 1,000 population in a year against children per woman in a lifetime

questions.q: A minister says: 'Our country's population today is the result of last year's births alone.' Which correction agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: It results from years of gradual change in births, deaths and the movement of people
o: It results from years of gradual change in births, deaths and the movement of people
It results from the number of deaths alone, since deaths decide how many people remain alive each year
It results from births and fertility together, since the movement of people leaves the total unchanged
It results from the latest census, which fixes the size of the population until the next count

questions.q: Each woman in a group of 5,000 women has, on average, the replacement level fertility rate that the chapter gives. Together the group has ___ children in all.

Write a short situation, with illustrative figures per 1,000 people, of a town where births exceed deaths and yet the population falls. Name the indicator of Fig. 6.7 responsible, and show the arithmetic.
questions.a: Sample: In a town there are 14 births and 9 deaths for every 1,000 people in a year, so births exceed deaths by 5. But 8 people per 1,000 leave the town for work elsewhere. The change is 5 - 8 = -3 per 1,000, a fall. The indicator responsible is migration, the movement of people from one place to another.
s: Gives births above deaths with figures
Gives a larger movement out and the net fall of 3 per 1,000
Names migration as the indicator

questions.q: Town A has 20,000 people and records 300 births in a year; Town B has 50,000 people and records 650 births. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Town A has the higher birth rate, although Town B recorded more births
o: Town A has the higher birth rate, although Town B recorded more births
Town B has the higher birth rate, since 650 is greater than 300
The two towns have equal birth rates, since both rates are stated for one year
Town B has the higher birth rate, since a bigger town always has more babies per 1,000

questions.q:
(a) A district of 3,60,000 people records 4,320 live births in a year. Find its birth rate.
(b) A second district of 2,40,000 people records 3,360 live births. Which district has the higher birth rate, and what does the chapter say a higher birth rate means for the pace of growth?
questions.a: (a) 4,320 divided by 360 thousand is 12 per 1,000. (b) The second district: 3,360 divided by 240 thousand is 14 per 1,000, which is higher. The chapter says that when many babies are being born the birth rate is high and the population will grow faster.
s: (a) 12 per 1,000 with the working
(b) 14 per 1,000 for the second district, and the link of a higher birth rate to faster growth

questions.q:
Town P has 60,000 people and records 840 live births and 420 deaths in a year. Town Q has 90,000 people and records 1,260 live births and 810 deaths. Ignore migration.
(a) Find each town's birth rate and death rate per 1,000.
(b) Find the excess of births over deaths per 1,000 in each town.
(c) Which town adds more people in the year, and which one grows faster in proportion to its size?
(d) Explain how both answers in (c) can be true.
questions.a: (a) P: birth rate 840 / 60 = 14 and death rate 420 / 60 = 7. Q: birth rate 1,260 / 90 = 14 and death rate 810 / 90 = 9. (b) P: 14 - 7 = 7 per 1,000. Q: 14 - 9 = 5 per 1,000. (c) Q adds more people, 1,260 - 810 = 450 against 840 - 420 = 420 for P, but P grows faster in proportion, at 7 against 5 per 1,000. (d) Q has more people, so a smaller excess per 1,000 still makes a bigger number; the rate compares births and deaths with the size of the population.
s: Birth rates 14 and 14, death rates 7 and 9
Excess 7 and 5 per 1,000
Q adds 450 against 420, P grows faster in proportion
Explains that a rate compares with population size, so the two results differ

questions.q: A friend says: 'Country K has a high birth rate, so its population must be huge.' Using the unit in which the chapter states the birth rate, show why this does not follow.
questions.a: The birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 population in a year, so it compares births with the size of the population. A small country can have many births for every 1,000 of its people and still have few people in all, so a high rate does not tell the size.
s: States that the birth rate is per 1,000 population
Shows a high rate can belong to a small population

questions.q: A country has 20 births and 12 deaths for every 1,000 people in a year, and 10 people per 1,000 leave it to settle abroad. Which description is correct?
questions.a: Its population falls by 2 per 1,000, since the 10 who leave outweigh the 8 of natural gain
o: Its population falls by 2 per 1,000, since the 10 who leave outweigh the 8 of natural gain
Its population grows by 8 per 1,000, because births exceed deaths and people leaving do not count at all
Its population grows by 18 per 1,000, because births and the people leaving are both added to the total
Its population stays stable, because births are higher than deaths and the 10 who leave make no difference

questions.q:
India's fertility rate fell from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025, according to the chapter, which also says that India's population is still growing. The chapter says a fertility rate below 2.1 means a population might shrink over time, and the chapter also says a country's population is the result of years of gradual change in births, deaths and movement of people.
(a) How far below the replacement level was India's fertility rate in 2025?
(b) The chapter's rule seems to say India's population might shrink, yet it is growing. Give the part of the chapter's wording that removes the contradiction.
(c) What does the chapter say a country does when its people keep having fewer children for a long time?
(d) Predict, using only the chapter's statements, what the population of a country in India's position will eventually do if its fertility rate stays at 1.9.
questions.a: (a) 2.1 - 1.9 = 0.2 below the replacement level. (b) The words 'might shrink over time' and 'years of gradual change': a fertility rate below 2.1 does not make the population shrink at once, so growth can continue for now. (c) If people keep having fewer children, the country's population might stop growing or even start falling. (d) Growth should slow, then stop, and the population might begin to fall.
s: Part (a): 0.2 below
Part (b): 'might' and 'over time' remove the contradiction
Part (c): stop growing or even start falling
Part (d): predicts slowing, stopping and a possible fall, not an immediate fall

questions.q:
(a) 600 women have completed their child-bearing years and had 1,140 children in all. Find their fertility rate as the chapter defines it.
(b) Explain why this figure does not mean that each of the 600 women had exactly that number of children.
questions.a: (a) 1,140 / 600 = 1.9 children per woman. (b) The fertility rate is an average: some women will have had more children and some fewer, so the figure describes the group and not any one woman.
s: (b) Says it is an average, so individual women differ

questions.q:
A newspaper table (illustrative figures) gives Borea, a country whose fertility rate is 1.4: 9 births and 10 deaths for every 1,000 people in a year, and a net arrival of 6 migrants for every 1,000 people. An editor writes, 'Borea's low fertility is not hurting it: its population is rising'.
(a) By how much, per 1,000 people, does Borea's population change in the year, counting births, deaths and migrants?
(b) Is Borea's fertility rate above or below the replacement level, and what does the chapter say that suggests?
(c) What would the yearly change per 1,000 be if the migrants stopped arriving?
(d) Judge the editor's remark. Is the rising population evidence that the low fertility is harmless?
questions.a: (a) 9 - 10 + 6 = 5 per 1,000, a rise. (b) Below, since 1.4 is less than 2.1; the chapter says such a population might shrink over time. (c) 9 - 10 = -1 per 1,000, a fall. (d) The remark is not sound. The rise comes entirely from migration, one of the three causes of change in the chapter; births and deaths alone would make Borea's population fall, so the low fertility has a real effect that migration is hiding.
s: Part (a): rise of 5 per 1,000
Part (b): below 2.1, so might shrink
Part (c): fall of 1 per 1,000
Part (d): judges the remark unsound because migration alone causes the rise

questions.q: Rohit leaves his village in one district of Kerala and settles in a town in another district of Kerala for work. How does the chapter's definition of migration treat his move?
questions.a: It is migration, because migration can be within the country as well as outside it
o: It is migration, because migration can be within the country as well as outside it
It is not migration, because migration means crossing the border of the country, not moving between districts
It is migration only if he later moves on to settle in a town in another state of India
It is not migration, because migration is counted only when a whole family moves together

questions.q: Using the chapter, trace the chain that starts with women having fewer children and ends with a country whose population falls. Name each link, and say which words in the chapter show the process is not sudden.
questions.a: Women have fewer children, so the fertility rate falls. A lower fertility rate makes the birth rate drop. A lower birth rate slows down population growth. If people keep having fewer children, the country's population might stop growing or even start falling. The words 'over time' and 'if people keep having fewer children' show that this is gradual.
s: Names fertility falling, then birth rate dropping
Names slower growth, then stopping or falling
Identifies 'over time' and 'if people keep' as the words showing gradual change

questions.q:
Four countries have these fertility rates (illustrative): Aldoria 3.4, Bevland 2.1, Corsia 1.5, Dunmark 2.6.
(a) Sort them into those likely to grow, those at the stable level and those that might shrink.
(b) Rank the four from the one furthest above 2.1 to the one furthest below it.
(c) Explain, in your own words, why Bevland's number is called the replacement level.
(d) Why should the words 'likely' and 'might' be kept in your sorting?
questions.a: (a) Aldoria and Dunmark are above 2.1 and likely to grow; Bevland is at 2.1 and stable; Corsia is below 2.1 and might shrink. (b) Aldoria, Dunmark, Bevland, Corsia. (c) 2.1 is the number of children needed to replace the parents in the population, so a country at this figure just keeps its population stable. (d) The chapter says above 2.1 the population is 'likely' to grow and below 2.1 it 'might' shrink over time, so the rate points to a direction but does not guarantee it.
s: Sorts the countries into the three groups correctly
Ranks Aldoria, Dunmark, Bevland, Corsia by distance above or below 2.1
Explains 2.1 as the number needed to replace the parents
Explains why 'likely' and 'might' are kept

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the chapter's definitions.
1. The birth rate is usually stated as the total number of live human births per 1,000 population in a year.
2. The death rate, also called the mortality rate, is typically expressed as deaths per 1,000 people.
3. The death rate is the number of deaths of children under five years of age per 1,000 live births.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
(a) A district of 6,00,000 people records 5,400 deaths in a year. Find its death rate.
(b) A second district of 2,50,000 people records 2,500 deaths. Which has the higher death rate, and which recorded more deaths?
questions.a: (a) 5,400 divided by 600 thousand is 9 deaths per 1,000 people. (b) The second district has the higher death rate, 2,500 divided by 250 thousand is 10 per 1,000, while the first recorded more deaths, 5,400 against 2,500.
s: (b) Second district higher in rate at 10, first higher in number of deaths

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A fall in a country's fertility rate slows down its population growth.
Reason (R): When women have fewer children, the birth rate also drops.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: A student's notes on the chapter's definitions contain one statement that mixes up two indicators. Which one?
questions.a: Fertility rate tells the number of babies born per 1,000 people in a year
o: Fertility rate tells the number of babies born per 1,000 people in a year
Fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime
Birth rate is stated as live births per 1,000 population in a year
When the fertility rate falls, the birth rate also drops

questions.q: A student says: 'China brought in its One-Child Policy in 1979 because its economy was slowing down for lack of workers.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: No: the worry was that fast growth would cause shortages of food, jobs and housing; a shortage of workers is a later effect
o: No: the worry was that fast growth would cause shortages of food, jobs and housing; a shortage of workers is a later effect
Yes: the chapter says a shortage of younger workers was what the government wanted to cure
No: the chapter says the policy was brought in because the elderly share had already risen to 26 per cent
Yes: the chapter says the economy was slowing in 1979, so families were fined to raise the number of workers

questions.q: A speaker says: 'In 2050 China will have about 14 per cent of its 1.31 billion people above 65.' Show, using the chapter, that this figure of elderly people is too small, and find by how many millions.
questions.a: The chapter expects the elderly share to be 26 per cent in 2050, not 14 per cent, which was the 2023 figure. 26 per cent of 1,310 million is 340.6 million, while 14 per cent is 183.4 million. The speaker's number is too small by 157.2 million.
s: States that the 2050 share is expected to be 26 per cent and 14 per cent belongs to 2023
Computes 340.6 million and 183.4 million
Finds the difference of 157.2 million

questions.q: Fig. 6.11 gives (fertility rate; women's literacy in per cent) for six states: Bihar (3.0; 55), Jharkhand (2.3; 61.7), Uttar Pradesh (2.4; 66.1), Karnataka (1.7; 73.4), Punjab (1.6; 79.4) and Delhi (1.6; 83.7). Which pair of states does NOT fit the pattern that the state with the higher women's literacy has the lower fertility rate?
questions.a: Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh
o: Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh
Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka
Punjab and Karnataka
Bihar and Jharkhand

questions.q:
Fig. 6.11 gives (fertility rate; literacy rate among women in per cent) for six states: Bihar (3.0; 55), Jharkhand (2.3; 61.7), Uttar Pradesh (2.4; 66.1), Karnataka (1.7; 73.4), Punjab (1.6; 79.4) and Delhi (1.6; 83.7). A student writes, 'The table proves that educating women is the one cause of lower fertility.'
(a) Arrange the states from lowest to highest women's literacy and read off their fertility rates in that order.
(b) Name the two steps in that order where fertility does not fall as literacy rises.
(c) Say what these two places show about the student's word 'one'.
(d) Judge whether the table can prove that education causes lower fertility. Use the chapter's wording.
questions.a: (a) Bihar 3.0, Jharkhand 2.3, Uttar Pradesh 2.4, Karnataka 1.7, Punjab 1.6, Delhi 1.6. (b) From Jharkhand to Uttar Pradesh the fertility rate rises, from 2.3 to 2.4, and from Punjab to Delhi it stays at 1.6. (c) Because the pattern is not exact, literacy cannot be the only thing affecting fertility; the chapter names other factors such as formal jobs and urbanisation with a high cost of living. (d) No. The table shows a relationship between two indicators for six states, which the chapter itself asks students to observe, but it does not prove cause and effect.
s: Part (a): the correct order of states and fertility values
Part (b): Jharkhand to Uttar Pradesh, and Punjab to Delhi
Part (c): other factors act too, so 'one' is wrong
Part (d): a relationship, not proof of cause

questions.q:
The chapter says many factors have contributed to falling fertility and birth rates, and gives several.
(a) Name any two of them and, for each, say how it leads to smaller families.
(b) Fig. 6.11 gives (fertility rate; women's literacy in per cent) for six states: Bihar (3.0; 55), Jharkhand (2.3; 61.7), Uttar Pradesh (2.4; 66.1), Karnataka (1.7; 73.4), Punjab (1.6; 79.4) and Delhi (1.6; 83.7). By how many points do the two women's literacy rates and the two fertility rates of Bihar and Delhi differ?
(c) A student says: 'The difference in women's literacy alone explains why Bihar's fertility is 3.0 and Delhi's 1.6.' Judge this statement using the chapter's word 'many'.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: better access to quality education, especially for girls, so that women who study and work in formal jobs marry later and have fewer children; women working in formal jobs, who likewise marry later and have fewer children; rapid urbanisation with a high cost of living in cities, so people prefer smaller families. (b) Literacy differs by 83.7 - 55 = 28.7 points and fertility by 3.0 - 1.6 = 1.4 points. (c) The statement goes too far. The chapter says many factors contribute, and the table shows only that lower fertility goes with higher women's literacy across states; literacy may well be one cause, but 'alone' is not shown.
s: First factor named (girls' education, women's formal jobs with later marriage, or urbanisation) with how it leads to smaller families
Second factor named, a different one, with how it leads to smaller families
Differences of 28.7 and 1.4 points
Judges 'alone' as unsupported because the chapter says many factors

questions.q: The chapter expects the share of China's population above 65 years to rise by ___ percentage points between 2023 and 2050.
Ria says: 'China's fertility rate has stayed above the replacement level since it ended the One-Child Policy in 2015, because it now allows up to three children.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says China ended the policy in 2015 and now allows up to three children, but its fertility rate still remains below replacement level, and its fertility rate was only 1 in 2025, far below 2.1. Allowing more children is not the same as people having more children.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Quotes that fertility still remains below replacement level
Uses the 2025 figure of 1 against 2.1

questions.q:
The fertility rates in Fig. 6.11 are Bihar 3.0, Uttar Pradesh 2.4, Jharkhand 2.3, Karnataka 1.7, Punjab 1.6 and Delhi 1.6.
(a) By how much does the fertility rate of Bihar exceed that of Delhi?
(b) How many of the six states have a fertility rate below the replacement level of 2.1? Name them.
questions.a: (a) 3.0 - 1.6 = 1.4. (b) Three states, Karnataka (1.7), Punjab (1.6) and Delhi (1.6), are below 2.1; Bihar (3.0), Uttar Pradesh (2.4) and Jharkhand (2.3) are above it.
s: (b) Three states, correctly named

questions.q: Leena says: 'In the table of Fig. 6.11, as women's literacy rises, the fertility rate generally falls, although the pattern is not perfectly regular.' Fig. 6.11 gives (fertility rate; women's literacy in per cent) for six states: Bihar (3.0; 55), Jharkhand (2.3; 61.7), Uttar Pradesh (2.4; 66.1), Karnataka (1.7; 73.4), Punjab (1.6; 79.4) and Delhi (1.6; 83.7). Test her statement against these figures.
questions.a: Yes. Bihar has the lowest literacy, 55 per cent, and the highest fertility, 3.0; Delhi has the highest literacy, 83.7 per cent, and a fertility of 1.6, among the lowest. The pattern is not perfectly regular: Uttar Pradesh, with 66.1 per cent, has fertility 2.4, higher than Jharkhand's 2.3 at 61.7 per cent, and Punjab and Delhi both have 1.6 despite different literacy.
s: Verdict: Yes, she is right
Supports the general pattern with Bihar and Delhi
Names an irregularity such as Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand, or Punjab and Delhi

questions.q: True or False? 'Ending the One-Child Policy in 2015 and allowing up to three children did not by itself bring China's fertility rate back to the replacement level.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that although China ended the policy in 2015 and now allows up to three children, its fertility rate still remains below replacement level, which it takes as a sign of the policy's lasting impact on society and the economy.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: fertility still remained below replacement level even after the policy ended

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter mean by kinship networks?
(b) Using that meaning, explain why a generation of children without siblings has fewer of them.
questions.a: (a) A kinship network is an interconnected web of social relationships through blood, marriage and adoption. (b) Brothers and sisters are relations by blood, and through them come further relations by marriage and adoption, so a child with no siblings has fewer of these links.
s: (a) Defines kinship networks as a web of relationships through blood, marriage and adoption
(b) Links siblings to blood relationships and the wider web that follows

questions.q:
Assertion (A): China's fertility rate was higher in 2025 than it was in 1963.
Reason (R): China's population peaked at 1.43 billion in 2022 and has started to shrink.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false

questions.q: A researcher plans to interview adults in China who were born in the years after 1979. According to the chapter, which experience is she most likely to find common among them?
questions.a: Having grown up without siblings and the kinship networks they bring
o: Having grown up without siblings and the kinship networks they bring
Having grown up in the largest families in the world
Having been told to stop at two children by a campaign begun in 1952
Having been fined for being born as the third child in the family

questions.q: A couple in Bengaluru are both in formal jobs; the wife studied up to a degree, they married when she was 29, and they plan one child because rent and school fees are high. Which set of factors named in the chapter do their choices illustrate?
questions.a: Women's education and formal jobs, and the high cost of living in cities
o: Women's education and formal jobs, and the high cost of living in cities
Fines imposed by the government on families that had a second child
A rise in child deaths that made parents plan for fewer children to be born
Joint family support that made large families too hard to manage at home

questions.q:
A newspaper table (illustrative) lists three countries. Aland: fertility rate 2.9, no population-control campaign, population rising. Borland: fertility rate 1.2, families fined for a second child for thirty years, population falling. Cania: fertility rate 1.9, a campaign urging no more than two children but no fines, population still rising for now. A columnist writes: 'Only fines can push a country's fertility rate below 2.1.'
(a) Which country resembles China in the chapter's account, and which resembles India?
(b) Which of the three have a fertility rate below the replacement level of 2.1?
(c) By the 2.1 rule alone, which is likely to grow over time and which might shrink?
(d) Judge the columnist's sentence using the table.
questions.a: (a) Borland resembles China (fines, a very low fertility rate, a falling population); Cania resembles India (a campaign urging two children, fertility 1.9, population still rising for now). (b) Borland and Cania. (c) Aland, at 2.9, is likely to grow; Borland and Cania, below 2.1, might shrink over time. (d) The sentence is wrong: Cania is below 2.1 with a campaign and no fines, and the chapter names education, formal jobs and urbanisation as other factors, so fines are not the only way.
s: Part (a): Borland like China and Cania like India
Part (b): Borland and Cania
Part (c): Aland likely to grow; Borland and Cania might shrink
Part (d): rejects 'only' using Cania and the other factors

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
1. China's One-Child Policy of 1979 allowed most families only one child, and families that broke the rule faced fines or job loss.
2. India's fertility rate fell from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025, which is above the replacement level.
3. China's share of elderly people, those above 65, is expected to rise sharply by 2050, which the chapter says could speed up the country's economic growth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
(a) Between 1950 and 2025, by how many points did India's fertility rate fall, and by what percentage of its 1950 value, to one decimal place?
(b) In which year did the 'Hum do humare do' campaign begin, and what did it emphasise?
questions.a: (a) 5.7 - 1.9 = 3.8 points, and 3.8 / 5.7 = 66.7 per cent of its 1950 value. (b) It began in 1952 and emphasised not having more than two children.
s: (a) 3.8 points and 66.7 per cent
(b) 1952 and not more than two children

questions.q:
Use the chapter's figures. China's fertility rate fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025; India's fell from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025.
(a) Find each country's fall in points and as a percentage of its starting value, to one decimal place.
(b) State which of the two countries' 2025 figures is further below the replacement level, and by how much each is below.
(c) The chapter describes China's measure of 1979 and India's of 1952 differently. State how.
(d) Say what the figures cannot tell you about how much of each fall was caused by the government measure.
questions.a: (a) China: 7.5 - 1 = 6.5 points, 6.5 / 7.5 = 86.7 per cent. India: 5.7 - 1.9 = 3.8 points, 3.8 / 5.7 = 66.7 per cent. (b) China's 1 is 1.1 below 2.1, and India's 1.9 is 0.2 below it, so China's is further below. (c) China's One-Child Policy allowed most families only one child, with fines or job loss for breaking it; India's 'Hum do humare do' campaign emphasised not having more than two children. (d) The figures do not separate the effect of the measure from the other causes the chapter names, such as education, formal jobs for women and urbanisation, so the share due to the measure is not known.
s: Falls of 6.5 and 3.8 points, and 86.7 and 66.7 per cent
China 1.1 below and India 0.2 below, China further
Contrasts one child with fines or job loss against at most two children
Says other causes mean the effect of the measure cannot be separated

questions.q: A student writes: 'India's fertility rate fell only because of the government campaign.' Name two other causes the chapter gives, and say what the word 'only' gets wrong.
questions.a: Improved access to education, especially for girls, with women in formal jobs marrying later and having fewer children, and rapid urbanisation with a high cost of living, which makes people prefer smaller families. The chapter says many factors have contributed to falling fertility, so 'only' ignores them.
s: Names two other causes from the chapter
Says the chapter gives many factors, so 'only' is wrong

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the item in Column B that it illustrates.
Column A: 1. A woman finishes college, takes a bank job and marries at 30  2. A Mumbai family chooses one child because rent and school fees are high  3. In the 1950s, posters urge families to stop at two children  4. A Chinese child born after 1979 has no brothers or sisters
Column B: a. rapid urbanisation with a high cost of living  b. formal education and formal jobs for women  c. the 'Hum do humare do' campaign  d. a generation without siblings and kinship networks

India's child mortality was 271 per 1,000 live births in 1950 and 28 in 2023, and life expectancy at birth rose from 30 years to 70 years.
(a) For 1,00,000 live births, find the number of children under five who would die at 271 per 1,000 and at 28 per 1,000.
(b) Find the fall in the number of deaths and the fall as a percentage of the 1950 figure, to one decimal place.
(c) Life expectancy at birth rose from 30 years to 70 years. Find the rise in years and as a percentage of 30.
(d) Say what both changes indicate about India, using the chapter's words.
questions.a: (a) At 271 per 1,000: 27,100 deaths; at 28 per 1,000: 2,800 deaths. (b) The fall is 24,300 deaths, which is 24,300 / 27,100 = 89.7 per cent. (c) The rise is 40 years, which is 40 / 30 = 133.3 per cent. (d) A lower mortality rate indicates the availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition, and the rise in life expectancy shows that newborns can now expect to live far longer on average.
s: 27,100 and 2,800 deaths
Fall of 24,300 and 89.7 per cent
Rise of 40 years and 133.3 per cent
Links the changes to quality healthcare and better nutrition

questions.q: After floods ruin their fields, a family from a district in Bihar moves to a city where the father finds a construction job. Which pair of reasons for migration named in the chapter do their circumstances show?
questions.a: A natural disaster and the search for better employment
o: A natural disaster and the search for better employment
Political instability and the search for education
Education and a natural disaster
Political instability and the search for better employment

questions.q: Name two reasons people migrate, as given in the chapter, and name the two circumstances that the chapter says can push people to move.
questions.a: People migrate for better employment opportunities and for education. The chapter says that natural disasters and political instability in an area can push people to migrate.
s: Names two valid reasons, for example employment and education, or a disaster
Names natural disasters and political instability as the circumstances that push people

questions.q:
The chapter defines life expectancy as the years a newborn is expected to live 'if they grow up with the same health, safety and living conditions' that people in their country have today.
(a) What does this assume about the future?
(b) Why might the actual average life of babies born in 2024 turn out different from 70?
questions.a: (a) It assumes that health, safety and living conditions stay as they are today. (b) If those conditions improve the babies may live longer on average, and if they worsen they may live shorter lives, so the average can differ from 70.
s: (a) States the assumption that conditions stay as today's
(b) Explains that better or worse conditions change the average

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's child mortality of 271 in 1950 meant that more than 250 of every 1,000 children born alive died before turning five.
Reason (R): Child mortality is the number of deaths of children under 5 years of age per 1,000 live births.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q:
Town T (illustrative) has 2,00,000 people. In one year 12,000 migrants arrive and 4,000 people leave. Its water works can serve at most 2,06,000 people.
(a) Find the net gain from migration and express it as a percentage of the town's population at the start.
(b) If nothing else changed that year, by how many people would the town exceed what its water works can serve at the end of the year?
(c) Name the indicator of Fig. 6.7 that is changing the town's population here.
(d) Using the chapter, name two pressures such a growth can create beyond water.
questions.a: (a) 12,000 - 4,000 = 8,000, and 8,000 / 2,00,000 = 4 per cent. (b) The town would have 2,08,000 people, which exceeds 2,06,000 by 2,000. (c) Migration. (d) Pressure on resources such as air and land, and strain on services such as transportation and housing.
s: Net gain of 8,000 and 4 per cent
Exceeds the water works by 2,000
Names migration
Names two pressures beyond water: air, land, transportation or housing

questions.q: A student reads 'India's child mortality was 28 in 2023' and says that 28 per cent of children died before the age of five. Show that this cannot be right, and say which year's figure it would be close to.
questions.a: Child mortality is the number of deaths of children under five per 1,000 live births, so 28 means 28 in every 1,000, which is 2.8 per cent. 28 per cent would be 280 per 1,000. That is close to the 1950 figure of 271 per 1,000, so her reading mixes up the 2023 figure with the situation of 1950.
s: States the unit: deaths under five per 1,000 live births
Converts 28 per 1,000 to 2.8 per cent and 28 per cent to 280 per 1,000
Compares with 271 per 1,000 in 1950

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
1. Child mortality is the number of deaths of children of all ages per 1,000 people in a year.
2. Life expectancy is the number of years after which every person born today will die.
3. A very large population concentrated in a limited area can put pressure on resources like water, air and land.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Town U has 50,000 people. Every year it records 800 births and 700 deaths, and 3,000 migrants arrive. If this continues unchanged for five years, what will its population be, and why?
questions.a: 65,500, since it gains 100 from births and deaths and 3,000 from arrivals each year
o: 65,500, since it gains 100 from births and deaths and 3,000 from arrivals each year
50,500, since only births and deaths change a town's population
65,000, since arrivals add to the population but births and deaths cancel out
53,500, since the arrivals are counted only in the first year

questions.q: A reader says: 'India's child mortality fell from 271 to 28, so India's death rate must now be 28 per 1,000 people.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: No: child mortality counts deaths of under-fives per 1,000 live births, the death rate all deaths per 1,000 people
o: No: child mortality counts deaths of under-fives per 1,000 live births, the death rate all deaths per 1,000 people
Yes: child mortality and the death rate are the same measure under two names, so 28 applies to both
No: child mortality counts deaths of people of all ages per 1,000 live births, not of under-fives
Yes: the death rate is the child mortality of the latest year, expressed per 1,000 people

questions.q: A councillor says: 'Our district's death rate has fallen, so we can close the primary health centre.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter reads a lower mortality rate as a sign that quality healthcare and better nutrition are available, so the centre is not unnecessary
o: The chapter reads a lower mortality rate as a sign that quality healthcare and better nutrition are available, so the centre is not unnecessary
The chapter says a lower mortality rate shows that healthcare is no longer needed in the district
The chapter says a mortality rate falls only when fewer babies are born in the district
The chapter says a lower death rate means that more people are migrating into the district

questions.q: India's child mortality in 1950, as the chapter gives it, applied to 20,000 live births means ___ children would die before the age of five.
A district reports 12,000 deaths in a year among 12,00,000 people. Which description matches the chapter's measure and its other name?
questions.a: 10 deaths per 1,000 people, the death rate, also called the mortality rate
o: 10 deaths per 1,000 people, the death rate, also called the mortality rate
10 deaths per 1,000 live births, which is child mortality
1 death per 1,000 people, the death rate
10 per cent, which is child mortality

questions.q:
City M (illustrative figures) had 100 lakh people in 2010 and 125 lakh in 2020. In those ten years its births exceeded its deaths by 1.5 lakh every year. A planner says, 'Most of City M's growth came from migration, so we should plan for newcomers first.'
(a) Find the total growth of City M in the ten years.
(b) Find the growth due to births and deaths together.
(c) Find the growth due to migration, as a share of the total growth.
(d) Judge the planner's statement and name two pressures the city's growth puts on its resources or services, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 125 - 100 = 25 lakh. (b) 1.5 lakh x 10 = 15 lakh. (c) 25 - 15 = 10 lakh from migration, which is 10 / 25 = 40 per cent. (d) The statement is wrong: migration gave 40 per cent of the growth and births and deaths gave 60 per cent, so migration was not the major part. The city's growth can pressure resources like water, air and land and strain services like transportation and housing.
s: Part (a): 25 lakh
Part (b): 15 lakh
Part (c): 10 lakh, which is 40 per cent
Part (d): judges the statement wrong with the 40 and 60 per cent split, and names two pressures

questions.q: Pooja says: 'Life expectancy has risen from 30 to 70 years, so every Indian born today will live to 70.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The rise from 30 years at independence to 70 years in 2024 is correct, but life expectancy is an average. The chapter says it does not mean every single person will live to exactly 70; it means that on average an Indian can expect to live up to 70, and it assumes today's health, safety and living conditions continue.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Accepts the figures 30 and 70 as correct
Explains it is an average under today's conditions, not a promise for each person

questions.q:
(a) A district's child mortality fell from 120 to 30 per 1,000 live births over thirty years. By how many deaths per 1,000 did it fall, and how many fewer under-five deaths is that among 5,000 live births?
(b) Which age group does child mortality count?
questions.a: (a) It fell by 120 - 30 = 90 per 1,000, so among 5,000 live births there are 5 x 90 = 450 fewer deaths. (b) Children under 5 years of age.
s: (a) 90 per 1,000 and 450 fewer deaths
(b) Children under 5 years of age

questions.q: Write a short account of a family that migrates for its children's education, using the chapter's meaning of migration. Then name two pressures on the place they move to if many other families do the same in a limited area.
questions.a: Sample: The Khan family leaves a small town and moves to Bengaluru to settle there, so that their two children can attend a better school; they plan to stay permanently. If many such families arrive in a limited area, the concentration of a very large population puts pressure on resources like water, air and land, and it strains services such as transportation and housing.
s: Describes a movement from one place to another to settle, for education
Names two pressures: any two of water, air, land, transportation, housing
Links the pressures to a large population in a limited area

questions.q: True or False? 'Only people who move to another country count as migrants in the chapter's meaning of migration.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter defines migration as the movement of people from one place to another within or outside a country, to settle either temporarily or permanently in the new location, so a move within the country counts too.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: migration covers movement within a country as well as outside it

questions.q:
Two sources describe India's life expectancy.
Source A (a speech): 'India's life expectancy is 70 years, so Indians die at 70.'
Source B (a school poster): 'Life expectancy at birth in India rose from 30 years at independence to 70 years in 2024. It is an average expectation for a newborn under today's conditions.'
(a) Which source agrees with the chapter?
(b) State the error in the other source.
(c) By how many times did life expectancy multiply between independence and 2024, to one decimal place?
(d) District P has a child mortality of 45 per 1,000 and District Q has 20 per 1,000. According to the chapter, which district shows better availability of healthcare and nutrition, and why?
questions.a: (a) Source B. (b) Source A treats an average as the age at which every person dies; the chapter says it does not mean every single person will live to exactly 70. (c) 70 / 30 = 2.33, about 2.3 times. (d) District Q, because a lower mortality rate indicates the availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition, and its child mortality of 20 is lower than P's 45.
s: Part (a): Source B
Part (b): average mistaken for everyone's age at death
Part (c): 2.3 times
Part (d): District Q, using lower mortality as the indicator

questions.q:
(a) State the chapter's meaning of migration.
(b) A family moves from a village to a district town in the same state. Does this count as migration under that meaning? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, within or outside a country, to settle either temporarily or permanently in the new location. (b) Yes, because the meaning includes movement within a country, and the family is moving to settle in a new place.
s: (a) States the meaning with within or outside a country and temporary or permanent settling
(b) Says yes, since movement within the country counts

questions.q:
Match each period or group in Column A with the description in Column B that fits it.
Column A: 1. India from 1901 to 1921  2. India after 1951  3. India after the mid-1980s  4. Italy, Japan and South Korea
Column B: a. death rate falls, birth rate stays high, rapid growth  b. both rates high, growth very slow  c. fertility begins to decline and is now below replacement level  d. fertility has dropped so far that the population is shrinking
A minister says: 'A country can reach Stage 3 only if the government restricts births by law.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter names economic development, healthcare, education and women's role in decisions as influences, and no law
o: The chapter names economic development, healthcare, education and women's role in decisions as influences, and no law
The chapter says a law restricting births is what moves every country from Stage 2 to Stage 3, whatever its income
The chapter says Stage 3 begins only when the death rate begins to rise again after a long fall
The chapter says countries reach Stage 3 only by raising the retirement age and using automation

questions.q: Arun says: 'Italy, Japan and South Korea are in Stage 3 and their populations are shrinking, so every country in Stage 3 must have a shrinking population.' Test his claim using the chapter's account of India.
questions.a: No. The chapter places India in Stage 3 after the mid-1980s, when its fertility rate began declining and fell below replacement level, yet it says India's population is still growing for now. Stage 3 slows growth; shrinking happens only if fertility drops significantly, as in Italy, Japan and South Korea.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Uses India after the mid-1980s as a Stage 3 country that is still growing
States that shrinking needs a significant drop in fertility, not just Stage 3

questions.q:
(a) State the two reasons the chapter gives for India being in Stage 1 from 1901 to 1921.
(b) Which one change in those reasons would, by the chapter's account of Stage 2, begin to lower the death rate?
questions.a: (a) Poor healthcare and low literacy among people. (b) The availability of better healthcare, which is how the death rate falls as nations progress economically.
s: (a) Poor healthcare and low literacy
(b) Better healthcare lowers the death rate

questions.q:
India's population was 361 million in 1951 and 683 million in 1981, according to Fig. 6.5.
(a) Find the increase as a percentage of the 1951 figure, to one decimal place.
(b) Name the stage the chapter assigns to India after 1951 and describe the birth and death rates in it.
(c) Name the stage and the two causes the chapter gives for India between 1901 and 1921.
(d) Explain why the percentage in (a) is so large for the stage in (b), compared with the stage in (c).
questions.a: (a) (683 - 361) / 361 = 89.2 per cent. (b) Stage 2: the death rate has fallen because of better healthcare, but the birth rate stays high. (c) Stage 1, because of poor healthcare and low literacy; both rates were high. (d) In Stage 2 the death rate has fallen while births stay high, so many more people are born than die, whereas in Stage 1 high deaths cancel most of the births and growth is very slow.
s: 89.2 per cent
Stage 2 with its rates described
Stage 1 with poor healthcare and low literacy
Explains the contrast using the gap between births and deaths

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Stage 2 of demographic transition a country's population grows rapidly.
Reason (R): In Stage 3 the death rate remains low while the birth rate begins to fall.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q:
The chapter places India in Stage 1 from 1901 to 1921, in Stage 2 after 1951, and says fertility began to decline after the mid-1980s. Take the mid-1980s as 1985.
(a) For how many years did Stage 1 last, and for how many years did India stay in Stage 2 before fertility began to decline?
(b) The chapter says nothing about 1921 to 1951. Why is it unsafe to say India stayed in Stage 1 through those years?
questions.a: (a) 1921 - 1901 = 20 years in Stage 1, and 1985 - 1951 = 34 years in Stage 2. (b) The chapter gives Stage 1 only for 1901 to 1921 and describes no birth and death rates for 1921 to 1951, and the stage depends on those rates, so a claim about those years is not supported.
s: (a) 20 years and 34 years
(b) Says the chapter is silent on 1921 to 1951 and the stage depends on the rates

questions.q: A student says: 'India was already in Stage 3 in 1951, because its fertility rate was already falling.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Wrong: the chapter places India in Stage 2 after 1951 and says fertility began to decline only after the mid-1980s
o: Wrong: the chapter places India in Stage 2 after 1951 and says fertility began to decline only after the mid-1980s
Right: the chapter says India entered Stage 3 in 1951, because deaths had fallen sharply and births had already begun to drop
Wrong: the chapter says India stayed in Stage 1 until 1985, when its death rate began to fall for the first time in its history
Right: the chapter says fertility fell below replacement level in 1951, as it has in Italy, Japan and South Korea

questions.q:
A student writes: 'In Stage 3 the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high, so the population grows rapidly.'
(a) Which stage does her sentence really describe?
(b) Rewrite the sentence so that it describes Stage 3 correctly.
questions.a: (a) Stage 2. (b) In Stage 3 the death rate remains low and the birth rate starts to decline, which slows overall population growth.
s: (a) Names Stage 2
(b) Gives Stage 3: death rate low, birth rate declining, growth slowing

questions.q: In India's Stage 1, from 1901 to 1921, healthcare was poor and literacy low. By the chapter's account of Stage 2, which change would have to come first for India to leave Stage 1?
questions.a: Better healthcare, so that the death rate falls while births stay high
o: Better healthcare, so that the death rate falls while births stay high
A fall in the birth rate, so that births drop below deaths
A rise in the death rate, so that it matches the high birth rate
A fall in literacy, so that families have more children

questions.q: Country Zeta had a high birth rate and a high death rate until new hospitals opened across it, after which its death rate fell sharply while its birth rate stayed high. Which stage of Fig. 6.12 has it entered, and what follows?
questions.a: Stage 2, with rapid population growth
o: Stage 2, with rapid population growth
Stage 1, with very slow or stagnant growth
Stage 3, with growth slowing down
Stage 3, with the population starting to shrink

questions.q: In Country Q fertility has dropped significantly, births are even lower, and the population has begun to shrink. Which reading agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Stage 3, as seen in Italy, Japan and South Korea
o: Stage 3, as seen in Italy, Japan and South Korea
Stage 3, as seen in Nigeria and Ethiopia
Stage 2, as seen in Italy, Japan and South Korea
Stage 1, as seen in India from 1901 to 1921

questions.q: The chapter says that in Stage 3 growth slows, but that the population 'starts to shrink' only 'if fertility drops significantly, leading to even lower births'. What does this tell you about a country in Stage 3 whose fertility has fallen only a little?
questions.a: Its population will not necessarily shrink. In Stage 3 the falling birth rate slows overall growth, but shrinking needs fertility to drop significantly, so a country with a small fall in fertility can go on growing, only more slowly.
