s: States that Stage 3 slows growth but does not by itself mean shrinking
Applies the condition of a significant fertility drop to the country with a small fall

questions.q: A student says that Country R, with a birth rate of 36 and a death rate of 34 per 1,000 people (illustrative), is in Stage 2 and is growing rapidly. Show that this cannot be right, and say which stage R fits.
questions.a: In Stage 2 the death rate has fallen well below the birth rate, which causes rapid growth. R's death rate of 34 is only 2 below its birth rate of 36, so a population of 10 lakh would grow by only 2,000 a year, which is very slow. Both rates are high and growth is very slow, so R fits Stage 1.
s: Notes that Stage 2 needs a fallen death rate with a high birth rate
Computes the gap of 2 per 1,000, or 2,000 a year on 10 lakh
Concludes R fits Stage 1 with very slow growth

questions.q:
Three countries have these rates per 1,000 people (illustrative): Alpha, birth rate 40 and death rate 38; Beta, birth rate 38 and death rate 12; Gamma, birth rate 11 and death rate 9.
(a) Place each country in a stage of Fig. 6.12.
(b) Find the natural increase per 1,000 for each.
(c) Alpha and Gamma have the same natural increase. Explain why this does not mean they are in the same stage.
(d) The chapter says a youth bulge is common in countries at a certain stage. Which of the three is the likeliest to have one?
questions.a: (a) Alpha is in Stage 1, Beta in Stage 2 and Gamma in Stage 3. (b) Alpha 2, Beta 26 and Gamma 2 per 1,000. (c) The stages depend on the combination of the rates and not on the gap alone: Alpha has both rates high, while Gamma has a low death rate and a birth rate that has fallen. (d) Beta, because the youth bulge is common in countries at Stage 2.
s: Correct stages for all three
Increases 2, 26 and 2
Explains that the combination of rates, not the gap, defines the stage
Beta, because a youth bulge is common at Stage 2

questions.q: Compare Stage 1 and Stage 2 in terms of the death rate, and say why one gives slow growth and the other rapid growth even though the birth rate is high in both.
questions.a: In Stage 1 the death rate is high, so deaths nearly cancel the many births and growth is very slow or stagnant. In Stage 2 the death rate has fallen while the birth rate is still high, so far more people are born than die and the population grows rapidly.
s: States the death rate is high in Stage 1 and has fallen in Stage 2
Explains that high deaths cancel births in Stage 1, but not in Stage 2

questions.q:
Fig. 6.5 gives India's population as 683 million in 1981, 846 in 1991, 1020 in 2001 and 1210 in 2011. The chapter places India in Stage 3 after the mid-1980s, a stage in which falling birth rates slow overall population growth. A student objects: 'India cannot be in Stage 3, because its population kept rising by more and more people every decade.'
(a) Find the increase in each of the three decades from 1981 to 2011.
(b) Express each as a percentage of the population at the start of that decade, to one decimal place.
(c) Which of the two quantities, the increase or the percentage, shows the 'slowing' of Stage 3?
(d) Judge the student's objection.
questions.a: (a) 163, 174 and 190 million. (b) 163 / 683 = 23.9 per cent; 174 / 846 = 20.6 per cent; 190 / 1020 = 18.6 per cent. (c) The percentage: it falls in each decade, while the increase keeps rising. (d) The objection fails. Stage 3 slows the pace of growth, it does not stop it, and the chapter says India's population is growing for now; the falling percentages are what the stage predicts.
s: Part (a): 163, 174 and 190 million
Part (b): 23.9, 20.6 and 18.6 per cent
Part (c): the percentage shows the slowing
Part (d): objection fails because Stage 3 slows growth without stopping it

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the stages of demographic transition.
1. In Stage 1 both the birth rate and the death rate are high, so population growth is very slow or stagnant.
2. In Stage 2 the death rate falls because of better healthcare, but the birth rate stays high, causing rapid population growth.
3. In Stage 3 the death rate remains low and the birth rate starts to decline, which slows overall population growth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A Class 6 student asks what 'demographic transition' means. Write a short explanation of your own that uses the comparison the chapter itself makes, and gives one line on each of the three stages.
questions.a: Sample: Just as a person passes through childhood, adulthood and old age, a country's population passes through phases. In the first stage both births and deaths are high, so the population hardly grows. In the second, deaths fall because of better healthcare but births stay high, so the population grows fast. In the third, deaths stay low and births begin to fall, so growth slows and may even turn into shrinking.
s: Uses the comparison with phases of an individual's life
Describes Stages 1 and 2 correctly
Describes Stage 3 correctly

questions.q:
Country K (illustrative) shows these figures per 1,000 people: in 1920, birth rate 40 and death rate 38; in 1960, birth rate 39 and death rate 20; in 2000, birth rate 22 and death rate 8; in 2040, birth rate 9 and death rate 10.
(a) Name the stage K is in for 1920 and for 1960.
(b) Find the natural change per 1,000 in each of the four years.
(c) In which year is K's population growing fastest, and which stage's description in the chapter explains this?
(d) What do the figures for 2040 show, and which countries named in the chapter resemble K in that year?
questions.a: (a) Stage 1 in 1920 and Stage 2 in 1960. (b) 1920: +2; 1960: +19; 2000: +14; 2040: -1 per 1,000. (c) 1960, because the death rate has fallen but the birth rate is still high, which is Stage 2 and causes rapid growth. (d) Births are now below deaths, so the population is shrinking, as in Italy, Japan and South Korea.
s: Part (a): Stage 1 and Stage 2
Part (c): 1960, explained by Stage 2
Part (d): shrinking, like Italy, Japan and South Korea

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
1. Sex ratio is the number of females per 1,000 males in the population, and it measures gender balance.
2. A population structure diagram whose widest part is the middle shows an ageing population.
3. In India's recent population pyramid the base has become narrower because families are having fewer children.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A student says a state has a sex ratio of 1,050 females per 1,000 males and that women are 48.5 per cent of its population. Show that both cannot be true together.
questions.a: With 1,050 females for every 1,000 males, the females are 1,050 out of 2,050 people, which is 1,050 / 2,050 = 51.2 per cent, not 48.5 per cent. The figure of 48.5 per cent goes with the ratio of 943 given for India in 2011, so the two statements contradict each other.
s: Converts the ratio of 1,050 into females out of 2,050 people
Computes 51.2 per cent
Concludes that 48.5 per cent matches 943, so the claims contradict

questions.q:
A national health body has 1,000 vaccination teams to distribute among states in proportion to their share of India's population in Fig. 6.13, where Uttar Pradesh has 16 per cent, Maharashtra 9, Bihar 9 and Kerala 3. The chapter also says Kerala and Tamil Nadu are experiencing significant population ageing compared with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.
(a) How many teams does each of the four states get?
(b) How many times as many teams does Maharashtra get as Kerala?
(c) Suppose the vaccine is meant for older people. Why might a distribution by population share alone not match the need? Use the chapter's point about ageing.
(d) Name the kind of information about a state's population, beyond its share, that the planners should obtain.
questions.a: (a) 1,000 x 16 / 100 = 160 for Uttar Pradesh, 90 for Maharashtra, 90 for Bihar and 30 for Kerala. (b) 90 / 30 = 3 times. (c) Share counts only how many people live in a state; Kerala is ageing faster than Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, so a larger part of its people may need a vaccine for older people than its share suggests. (d) The age structure, that is, how its population divides into children, working-age adults and the elderly.
s: Part (b): 3 times
Part (c): share ignores that Kerala is ageing faster
Part (d): age structure, the population composition

questions.q: Three population structure diagrams are shown. Diagram P is widest at the bottom, Diagram Q is widest in the middle, and Diagram R is widest at the top. Which set of readings agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: P: young and growing; Q: mostly working adults and stable; R: ageing
o: P: young and growing; Q: mostly working adults and stable; R: ageing
P: ageing; Q: mostly working adults and stable; R: young and growing
P: mostly working adults and stable; Q: young and growing; R: ageing
P: young and growing; Q: ageing; R: mostly working adults and stable

questions.q:
Country H (illustrative) had these shares of its people: under 15, 40 per cent; 15 to 59, 55 per cent; 60 and above, 5 per cent. Some decades later the shares are 27, 65 and 8 per cent.
(a) By how many percentage points did each group's share change?
(b) Which part of a population structure diagram (base, middle or top) does each group form, and what happened to its width?
(c) Name the shape the chapter gives to India's pyramid in recent years and say whether Country H now looks like it.
(d) Give the chapter's reasons for the narrower base and for the wider top.
questions.a: (a) Under 15: 27 - 40 = -13 points; 15 to 59: 65 - 55 = +10 points; 60 and above: 8 - 5 = +3 points. (b) The under-15 group forms the base, which has narrowed; the 15 to 59 group forms the middle, which has become much wider; the 60-and-above group forms the top, which has widened slightly. (c) Bell-shaped; yes, Country H now looks like it, with a narrower base, a much wider middle and a slowly widening top. (d) The base is narrower because families are having fewer children; the top is slowly widening because people live longer, owing to better healthcare, nutrition and living conditions.
s: Changes of -13, +10 and +3 points
Matches groups to base, middle and top with the widths
Names the bell shape and applies it to Country H
Gives both reasons: fewer children, and longer lives from better healthcare, nutrition and living conditions

questions.q:
The chapter gives India's life expectancy as around 30 to 35 years in the 1950s and as 30 years at independence.
(a) Are the two statements consistent? Explain.
(b) What would a life expectancy that low do to the top of the population structure diagram?
questions.a: (a) Yes: 30 years is the lowest value in the range of 30 to 35 years, so the two statements describe the same low level of life expectancy. (b) It would keep the top narrow, because few people lived long enough to be old, which agrees with the chapter's description of fewer older people in the narrow triangle.
s: (a) Says they are consistent because 30 lies within 30 to 35
(b) Says the top stays narrow, with fewer older people

questions.q: If a town of 3,000 males had the same number of females per 1,000 males as India in Census 2011, it would have ___ females.

A ward's census record says: (i) 3,000 residents live in sector A and 5,000 in sector B; (ii) 2,400 residents are female and 2,600 are male; (iii) 1,200 residents are graduates.
(a) Which entry shows geographical distribution, and which entries show population composition (structure)?
(b) Use the entry needed to find the ward's sex ratio, to the nearest whole number.
questions.a: (a) Entry (i) is geographical distribution; entries (ii) and (iii), gender and education, are population composition. (b) The sex ratio is females per 1,000 males, so 2,400 / 2,600 x 1,000 = 923.
s: (a) Entry (i) as distribution, and (ii) and (iii) as composition
(b) 923 females per 1,000 males

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A balanced sex ratio matters for a country's equitable development and social stability.
Reason (R): India's sex ratio of 943 females per 1,000 males in 2011 meant that women made up 50 per cent of the population.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q:
Town A has 4,800 males and 4,512 females. Town B has 6,000 males and 5,520 females (illustrative). India's sex ratio in 2011 was 943. A ratio of 1,000 means equal numbers of females and males.
(a) Find the sex ratio of each town.
(b) Find the share of females in each town's population, to one decimal place.
(c) Compare each town's ratio with India's 943.
(d) Which town is closer to a balanced sex ratio?
(e) Both ratios are below 1,000. What does that say about the numbers of females and males in each town?
questions.a: (a) A: 4,512 / 4,800 x 1,000 = 940; B: 5,520 / 6,000 x 1,000 = 920. (b) A: 4,512 / 9,312 = 48.5 per cent; B: 5,520 / 11,520 = 47.9 per cent. (c) A is 3 below India's 943 and B is 23 below it. (d) Town A is closer to a balanced ratio. (e) Both are below 1,000, so each town has fewer females than males.
s: Ratios 940 and 920
Female shares 48.5 and 47.9 per cent
A is 3 below and B 23 below 943
Names Town A as closer to balance
Says each town has fewer females than males

questions.q:
(a) Add the shares of the four largest states in Fig. 6.13: Uttar Pradesh 16, Maharashtra 9, Bihar 9 and West Bengal 8 per cent.
(b) What does the total say about how India's people are spread across its states?
questions.a: (a) 16 + 9 + 9 + 8 = 42 per cent. (b) Four states hold about two-fifths of the country's people, while the chapter says many states and union territories hold less than 1 per cent each, so the people are spread very unevenly across the states.
s: (a) 42 per cent
(b) Concludes that the distribution is uneven, with a few states holding a large share

questions.q: Describe in words the population structure diagram of a country that is ageing, like Japan: say which part is widest, which part is narrow, and what each part shows. Then say what this suggests the country will need more of, using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The top part is wide, showing many older people, and the base is narrower, showing fewer children being born; the middle shows the working adults. Since there are more older people than young adults, the country has an ageing population. The chapter says that a higher proportion of the elderly means more facilities for healthcare are required.
s: Describes a wide top and a narrower base
Says what the top and base show: many older people, fewer children
Links the elderly share to more healthcare facilities

questions.q: Sana says: 'India's sex ratio improved between 2001 and 2011, but even in 2011 there were fewer females than males, although a few states had a ratio of about 1,000 or more.' Test her statement against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter gives 933 in Census 2001 and 943 in 2011, so the ratio improved. 943 is below 1,000, so there were fewer females than males per 1,000, and the chapter names Kerala, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu as states that had over 1,000 or near 1,000.
s: Verdict: Yes, she is right
Confirms the improvement from 933 to 943 and that 943 is below 1,000
Names Kerala, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu as near or over 1,000

questions.q: A student reads that India's sex ratio was 943 in 2011 and writes, 'So there were 943 males for every 1,000 females.' Which correction agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: There were 943 females for every 1,000 males, so females were fewer than males
o: There were 943 females for every 1,000 males, so females were fewer than males
There were 943 females in every 1,000 people, so males were 57 in every 1,000
There were 943 females in every state, since the ratio is counted state by state
There were 943 males for every 1,000 females, and her statement is already correct

questions.q:
A school survey (illustrative) found that Village P had 4,100 males and 3,813 females in Census 2001, and 4,300 males and 4,128 females in Census 2011. India's figures were 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011. A ratio of 1,000 means equal numbers of females and males. The sarpanch says, 'Our sex ratio is now fully balanced.'
(a) Find Village P's sex ratio in each census year.
(b) By how much did P's ratio rise between the two years, and how does this compare with the rise for India?
(c) Find the share of females in P's population in 2011, to one decimal place, and compare it with India's 48.5 per cent.
(d) Judge the sarpanch's statement.
questions.a: (a) 2001: 3,813 / 4,100 x 1,000 = 930; 2011: 4,128 / 4,300 x 1,000 = 960. (b) P's ratio rose by 30, while India's rose by 10 (from 933 to 943). (c) 4,128 / 8,428 = 49.0 per cent, a little above India's 48.5 per cent. (d) The statement is not correct. P's ratio improved and is above India's 943, but at 960 it is still 40 below 1,000, so there are still fewer females than males and the ratio is not fully balanced.
s: Part (a): 930 and 960
Part (b): rise of 30 against India's 10
Part (c): 49.0 per cent against 48.5
Part (d): not fully balanced, because 960 is still 40 below 1,000

questions.q: A state's census shows 1,010 females for every 1,000 males, while the figure for India as a whole in 2011 was 943. Which statement agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The state has more females than males; Kerala, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu are named as having over 1,000 or near 1,000
o: The state has more females than males; Kerala, Puducherry and Tamil Nadu are named as having over 1,000 or near 1,000
The state has fewer females than males, since the chapter says no state has a ratio of 1,000 or more
The state has equal numbers of females and males, since a ratio above 943 is called balanced
The state has more females than males, and the chapter names Bihar and Uttar Pradesh as such states

questions.q: A classmate insists that a population pyramid really is a pyramid. Using the note printed beside the diagram, say what she has missed.
questions.a: The note says that although the term 'population pyramid' is used widely, the picture on paper looks more like a triangle whose parts have been pulled outwards or shrunk into different shapes. It is a three-dimensional idea drawn in two dimensions, so the shape need not be a true pyramid.
s: States that on paper it looks like a triangle whose parts are pulled out or shrunk
Says it is a 3-dimensional concept shown in 2 dimensions

questions.q:
Fig. 6.13 gives Uttar Pradesh 16 per cent of India's people and Kerala 3 per cent, and the chapter says Kerala's sex ratio was over 1,000 or near it while India's was 943.
(a) How many times as large is Uttar Pradesh's share as Kerala's?
(b) Does a state's share of India's population tell you anything about its sex ratio? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 16 / 3 is about 5.3 times. (b) No. The share says only how many of India's people live in the state, which is a matter of size and distribution; the sex ratio is a matter of composition. Kerala has a small share but a ratio over or near 1,000, above India's 943.
s: (a) About 5.3 times
(b) Says share is size and the sex ratio is composition, with Kerala as the example

questions.q: The shares of India's population by state, taken from Fig. 6.13, are: Uttar Pradesh 16 per cent, Maharashtra 9, Bihar 9, West Bengal 8, Madhya Pradesh 6, Tamil Nadu 6, Rajasthan 6, Karnataka 5, Gujarat 5, Andhra Pradesh 4, Odisha 3, Telangana 3, Kerala 3 and Delhi 1. Which group has the largest combined share?
questions.a: Maharashtra, Bihar and West Bengal
o: Maharashtra, Bihar and West Bengal
Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Karnataka
Uttar Pradesh, Kerala and Delhi
Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana and Kerala

questions.q: Which change between India's 1950s population pyramid and the one in recent years does the chapter describe?
questions.a: The base has narrowed and the middle has become much wider, while the top slowly widens
o: The base has narrowed and the middle has become much wider, while the top slowly widens
The base has become wider and the middle much narrower, while the top has shrunk to almost nothing
The middle has stayed the same while the base and the top have both become wider over time
The whole diagram has become a narrower triangle with more children at the bottom

questions.q:
Fig. 6.17 gives median ages: India 28, Japan 50, Italy 48, Germany 47, China 40 and the USA 39.
(a) By how many years does Germany's median age exceed that of the USA?
(b) Which of the other five countries has a median age closest to India's, and what does the size of the gap show about India's age structure?
questions.a: (a) 47 - 39 = 8 years. (b) The USA, at 39, is closest, yet it is 11 years above India's 28. Every one of the five is much older than India, which shows that India has a young population compared with these countries.
s: (a) 8 years
(b) The USA with a gap of 11 years, and the conclusion that India is much younger

questions.q: Anita works in a formal job in Pune, also cooks and looks after her two children, and has no daycare nearby or flexible hours. She thinks of leaving her job. Which term and which remedy does the chapter give for her situation?
questions.a: The 'double burden'; daycare centres, family support and flexible hours would help
o: The 'double burden'; daycare centres, family support and flexible hours would help
The 'youth bulge'; raising the retirement age for older workers would free her from work in the formal sector
The 'kinship network'; lowering the cost of living in the city would let her family afford more children
The 'demographic dividend'; having fewer taxpayers in the country would reduce what she is asked to do

questions.q: Fig. 6.17 gives the median age as 50 in Japan and 28 in India. Say which of the two the chapter would expect to feel pressure on healthcare and pensions sooner, and which to have a demographic dividend now, and explain how the median age points to this.
questions.a: Japan would feel the pressure on healthcare and pensions sooner, because a median age of 50 means a population with many older people, and the chapter says an ageing population strains healthcare and pension payments. India, with a median age of 28, has a large working-age population, which is what the chapter calls its demographic dividend.
s: Names Japan for the earlier pressure on healthcare and pensions
Names India for the demographic dividend
Links each to what the median age says about the age structure

questions.q: True or False? 'A larger working-age group means the government has less to spend, because more people need its services.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the working-age population earns money and pays taxes, and the government uses that money to build schools, hospitals, roads and parks, so a larger working-age group adds to what it can spend.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: workers pay taxes that the government spends on schools, hospitals, roads and parks

questions.q:
(a) Taking 27 per cent as under 15 and nearly 65 per cent as the 15-to-59 group (as the chapter gives them), what share is left, roughly?
(b) Which age group does that remainder stand for, on the chapter's band?
questions.a: (a) 100 - 27 - 65 = 8, so roughly 8 per cent. (b) Persons aged 60 and above, because the working-age band in the chapter is 15 to 59 and the under-15 group lies below it.
s: (a) About 8 per cent
(b) Persons aged 60 and above

questions.q: India's children under five peaked in number in 2007, and those under 15 peaked in 2011. Assume a child stays in the under-15 group from birth until her fifteenth birthday. Which reasoning explains why the larger age group peaked later?
questions.a: The group keeps rising until fewer children join it each year than leave it
o: The group keeps rising until fewer children join it each year than leave it
A child leaves the under-15 group at age five, so the group responds to births almost immediately
The under-15 group includes elderly people, whose numbers kept rising for years after 2007
Births kept rising after 2007, which pushed both groups up until 2011 and then stopped

questions.q: State E and State F each have 1 crore people. In E, 65 lakh are of working age; in F, 55 lakh. Which pair names the chapter's term for the growth potential of such an age structure and the state that has more of it?
questions.a: The demographic dividend; State E, with more working-age people
o: The demographic dividend; State E, with more working-age people
The youth bulge; State F, with fewer working-age people
The demographic dividend; State F, since fewer workers means lower costs
The double burden; State E, since more workers means more household duties

questions.q:
A student says: 'Once older people stop working, they contribute nothing to society.'
(a) Name two of the four phases of life in the concept of ashrama dharma that the chapter mentions.
(b) Using the chapter's point about older people, say why the student's sentence is wrong.
questions.a: (a) Any two of brahmacharya, grihastashrama, vanaprasta and sanyasa. (b) The chapter says that although older people begin to withdraw from economic activities, they continue to share knowledge and wisdom with family and society, for example in rituals and storytelling, and they hold knowledge that may not be in books.
s: (a) Names two valid phases
(b) Says older people continue to share knowledge and wisdom, so they do contribute

questions.q:
A state plans a skill-training programme for young people before the window of India's demographic dividend closes after 2050 (illustrative figures). Proposal 1 starts at the beginning of 2026, runs to the end of 2050 and trains 5 lakh youth a year. Proposal 2 starts at the beginning of 2041, runs to the end of 2050 and trains 12 lakh youth a year.
(a) How many youth does each proposal train by the end of 2050?
(b) Which proposal trains more by then, although its yearly number is smaller?
(c) The chapter gives 2007 and 2011 as the years in which the numbers of children under five and under 15 peaked. What does this suggest about the number of new young workers over the coming decades?
(d) Predict what the chapter says the country begins to face after 2050.
questions.a: (a) Proposal 1: 25 years x 5 lakh = 125 lakh. Proposal 2: 10 years x 12 lakh = 120 lakh. (b) Proposal 1, because it starts earlier and runs for more years. (c) Both groups of children have been falling since those peaks, so fewer young people will be coming up to enter the workforce, and waiting costs more of the window. (d) A transition towards an older population, with pressure on healthcare, fewer workers to replace those who retire, and difficulty paying pensions.
s: Part (a): 125 lakh and 120 lakh
Part (b): Proposal 1, with the reason of an earlier start
Part (c): falling numbers of children mean fewer new young workers
Part (d): an older population with pressure on healthcare, workers and pensions

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's demographic dividend will last indefinitely.
Reason (R): The chapter says the growth in India's young population is expected to decrease beyond 2050.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false

questions.q: A student says that in a state 38 per cent of the people are under 15 and 70 per cent are in the 15-to-59 group. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The two groups do not overlap, since one is under 15 and the other starts at 15. Together they would hold 38 + 70 = 108 per cent of the people, which is more than the whole population of 100 per cent, so the figures cannot both be true.
s: States that under 15 and 15 to 59 are separate groups
Adds to 108 per cent
Concludes this exceeds 100 per cent, so it is impossible

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the idea in Column B that it illustrates.
Column A: 1. A Japanese town opens community centres and uses robot assistants to help care for older adults  2. A government invests in good education, skilling and healthcare for its young people  3. A woman manages a formal job and also all the household duties  4. A grandmother guides her family's rituals and tells stories not found in books
Column B: a. harnessing the demographic dividend  b. the 'double burden'  c. preparing for an ageing society  d. the continuing role of older people

Country J (illustrative) has 1 crore people, of whom 65 per cent are of working age. The chapter's reasoning says this window is limited, and suppose that after it closes only 55 per cent are of working age. Each working-age person pays Rs 6,000 a year in taxes on average (illustrative).
(a) How many working-age people are there now, and how much tax do they pay in a year, in crore of rupees?
(b) How many are there after the window closes, and how much tax?
(c) By how much, and by what percentage of the first figure, does the tax fall?
(d) Which statement of the chapter does this illustrate, and what does the chapter say a government gains from the working-age group while the window lasts?
questions.a: (a) 65 lakh people pay 65,00,000 x 6,000 = Rs 3,900 crore. (b) 55 lakh people pay Rs 3,300 crore. (c) The fall is Rs 600 crore, which is 600 / 3,900 = 15.4 per cent. (d) It illustrates that the window of opportunity is limited because the population begins to move towards an older one after 2050; while it lasts, the working-age group earns money and pays taxes, which the government uses to build schools, hospitals, roads and parks.
s: 65 lakh and Rs 3,900 crore
55 lakh and Rs 3,300 crore
Fall of Rs 600 crore and 15.4 per cent
Links to the limited window and the move to an older population
States that taxes from the working-age group pay for schools, hospitals, roads and parks

questions.q: A developing country with a young population decides to copy Japan by raising its retirement age and using automation. Does that match the chapter's advice for such a country?
questions.a: No: developing countries are to harness the dividend through education, skilling and healthcare
o: No: developing countries are to harness the dividend through education, skilling and healthcare
Yes: the chapter says developing countries should first raise the retirement age
Yes: the chapter says automation is the only way to harness a dividend
No: the chapter says developing countries should discourage women from taking formal jobs

questions.q:
State P and State Q (illustrative) each have 1 crore people. In P, 28 per cent are under 15, 62 per cent are aged 15 to 59 and 10 per cent are aged 60 and above. In Q, 17 per cent are under 15, 60 per cent are 15 to 59 and 23 per cent are 60 and above. For this exercise assume that pensions are paid to those aged 60 and above and funded by taxes from those aged 15 to 59.
(a) Find how many persons aged 15 to 59 there are for every person aged 60 and above in P and in Q, to one decimal place.
(b) Which state's government will find paying pensions harder, and why, using the chapter?
(c) What does P's 28 per cent under 15 mean for the size of its future working-age group?
(d) Q's minister proposes raising the retirement age. Say whether Japan's experience in the chapter supports this as one step, and name one other Japanese step.
questions.a: (a) P: 62 / 10 = 6.2; Q: 60 / 23 = 2.6. (b) Q's, because it has fewer young taxpayers for each older person, and the chapter says an ageing population makes it harder for governments to pay pensions as there are fewer young taxpayers. (c) A large group of children will enter working age, giving P a larger future workforce. (d) Yes: Japan has raised the retirement age; it has also used technology and automation, with robots and AI assistants and community centres for older adults.
s: Part (a): 6.2 and 2.6
Part (b): Q, with fewer young taxpayers per older person
Part (c): many children will enter the working-age group, giving P a larger future workforce
Part (d): yes, Japan raised the retirement age, plus one other step

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
1. Taxes are a voluntary contribution that workers may choose to make to the government.
2. An ageing population puts pressure on healthcare systems and leaves fewer workers to replace those who retire.
3. For developing countries the chapter says the challenge is to harness the demographic dividend through investment in good education, skilling and healthcare.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
In a family in Pune (illustrative), Ms Rao spends 8 hours a day on her formal job and 4 hours on household duties; her husband spends 8 hours on his job and 1 hour on household duties.
(a) Find each person's total working hours in a day and the difference.
(b) What phrase does the chapter use for Ms Rao's situation?
(c) Name the three things whose lack, the chapter says, makes it harder for women like her to take part in the workforce.
(d) Say what the chapter expects supportive family systems and childcare infrastructure to do for the economy.
questions.a: (a) Ms Rao: 8 + 4 = 12 hours; her husband: 8 + 1 = 9 hours; she works 3 hours more. (b) The 'double burden'. (c) Childcare facilities, joint family support systems and flexible work hours. (d) They can help the economy turn its demographic dividend into lasting progress.
s: 12 hours, 9 hours and a difference of 3
Names the double burden
Names childcare facilities, joint family support and flexible work hours
States that these help turn the dividend into lasting progress

questions.q: In a state the share of people above 60 doubles over thirty years while the share of working-age people falls. Which consequence would the chapter predict for the government?
questions.a: Paying pensions and providing services becomes harder, because there are fewer young taxpayers
o: Paying pensions and providing services becomes harder, because there are fewer young taxpayers
Paying pensions becomes easier, because there are more elderly people to share the cost of the pensions between them
Schools become more crowded, because elderly people send more of their grandchildren to school
Healthcare needs fall, because older adults need fewer facilities than young adults and children do

questions.q: The chapter says Kerala and Tamil Nadu are experiencing significant population ageing as compared to Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. A student concludes: 'So Bihar will be the first of these states to face pressure on pensions and healthcare.' Judge her conclusion.
questions.a: It is not supported. The chapter says Kerala and Tamil Nadu are ageing faster than Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, and an ageing population puts pressure on healthcare and pensions, so these pressures should show first in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
s: Rejects the conclusion and names Kerala and Tamil Nadu as ageing faster
Links ageing to pressure on healthcare and pensions

questions.q: Japan's median age in Fig. 6.17 is ___ years higher than India's.
The chapter calls the demographic dividend a growth 'potential'. Using the chapter, name two things developing countries must do to turn this potential into lasting progress.
questions.a: They must invest in good education, skilling and healthcare. They also need supportive family systems and childcare infrastructure such as daycare centres, so that women with the 'double burden' can take part in the workforce.
s: Names investment in education, skilling and healthcare
Names childcare infrastructure or supportive family systems

questions.q: Kabir says: 'An ageing population puts pressure on healthcare systems, and it leaves more workers than before to replace those who retire.' Test his statement against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is correct: older adults need more healthcare, so healthcare systems are under pressure. The second half is wrong: an ageing population leaves fewer workers to replace those who retire, which can slow down the economy, and the chapter adds that governments find it harder to pay pensions and provide services because there are fewer young taxpayers.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts the pressure on healthcare
Corrects the second half: fewer workers replace those who retire, with the slower economy and pension difficulty
